The harbour at Whitby had changed little in forty years, or so the old men who still fished from it liked to claim whenever the weather turned and the pub filled up on a wet Tuesday afternoon. The trawlers were smaller now, and half the sheds along the quay sold fudge and postcards instead of nets, but the tide still came in twice a day and the gulls still screamed over the breakwater at first light. Children on the pier counted the boats and made up names for the ones whose paint had worn away.

By the spring the town had filled with visitors again. Families queued for ice cream on the pier, teenagers jumped off the wall at high tide, and the car park behind the arcade was full by ten in the morning. The shopkeepers were pleased. The fishermen were not. The harbour wall, they said, was crumbling, and the council had spent the winter arguing about whose budget should pay for the repairs. A surveyor from York had visited in February, taken photographs, measured the cracks with a brass gauge, and promised a report that never came.

Thomas Rowntree had been born in the cottage above the slipway and had gone to sea at fourteen, as his father and grandfather had done before him. He knew the run of the tide across the bar better than any chart, and he could name every wreck between the pier and the headland without pausing for breath. When the council announced that the old lifeboat station would be sold, he wrote three letters, attended two meetings, and stood in the rain outside the town hall with a placard that nobody photographed.

His nephew Michael, who had spent ten years in an office in Leeds and knew nothing about boats, arrived one weekend with plans for a restaurant. He talked about seasonal menus and local produce and the sort of prices that visitors from the city would happily pay, and he had already sketched a sign for the door. Thomas listened, said nothing, and walked down to the slipway to check the moorings.

It was not until the Sunday evening, with the fire lit and the wind rattling the windows, that Michael finally asked what he should do. The old man thought for a long moment, turned his glass slowly on the table, and then gave him the only advice he had: keep the boat, forget the restaurant, and find work that did not depend on other people's holidays. Michael laughed, but he wrote it down, and years later he would say that the note in his wallet had saved him from a great deal of trouble.
